notes: Adversarial regression suite. Each eval plants one trap from the Where Mistakes Hide table in its facts and is graded on its Must and Must not lines by a human or LLM judge. Every quantity the arithmetic depends on is defined in the prompt, no Must line depends on a [VERIFY] fact, every eval supplies the trigger document dates, the signer's authority and a statement that no criminal or fraud issue exists, so no Checkpoint A hard stop blocks the expected output. Dates were computed on October 30, 2026 with a script applying the IRC 7503 roll and the D.C. Code 28-2701 holiday list, and checked by hand. Eval 1 targets the notice of deficiency row (Sixth Circuit, Oquendo read in full); eval 2 the Form 872/872-A row; eval 3 the refund claim row; eval 4 the penalty file row (Eleventh Circuit, Kroner read in full); eval 5 the BBA NOPPA row. Re-check evals 1 and 4 if the Supreme Court or Congress (H.R. 5349) changes the petition-deadline or 6751(b) rules.

evals.name: petition-deadline-receipt-date-and-notice-date
evals.prompt: We represent Dana Ruiz under a Form 2848 covering her 2023 Form 1040 income tax. This is a civil exam only; there has been no contact from Criminal Investigation and no fraud penalty. The IRS notice of deficiency (Letter 3219) is dated October 20, 2026, and the certified mail list we obtained shows it was mailed that day to her Columbus, Ohio address, where she has lived since 2015. The notice was addressed in the United States. Its 'Last day to file a petition with the United States Tax Court' box reads January 22, 2027. Dana was traveling and first opened it on October 29, 2026. My associate counted 90 days from October 29 and calendared January 27, 2027, and says that even if we're late the Sixth Circuit allows equitable tolling, so there's no pressure. Today is October 30, 2026. Build the clocks register for the Tax Court petition and tell me what date to file by.
evals.expected_output: Computes the 6213(a) deadline from the October 20, 2026 mailing date (raw day 90 is Monday, January 18, 2027, Martin Luther King Jr. Day, rolled to Tuesday, January 19, 2027), separately records the January 22, 2027 date printed on the notice as a later safe harbor under the last sentence of 6213(a), rejects the January 27, 2027 receipt-based date, explains that Oquendo makes the deadline nonjurisdictional and tollable in the Sixth Circuit only case by case, and recommends filing by January 19, 2027. Hard stops checked: criminal exposure (none stated), no trigger document (supplied), improper request (none), no authority to sign (authority stated).
expected_behavior: Must: compute the statutory petition deadline from the October 20, 2026 mailing date, showing raw day 90 as Monday, January 18, 2027 (Martin Luther King Jr. Day, a D.C. legal holiday) and the due date as Tuesday, January 19, 2027.
Must: state that a petition filed on or before January 22, 2027, the last date specified in the notice, is treated as timely under the last sentence of IRC 6213(a).
Must: state that the 90-day period runs from mailing, not receipt, and that the associate's January 27, 2027 date is wrong.

Must: state that the Sixth Circuit (Oquendo v. Commissioner, 2025) holds the 6213(a) deadline nonjurisdictional and subject to equitable tolling, that tolling is decided case by case, and that the Tax Court itself treats the deadline as jurisdictional except where circuit precedent governs under Golsen.
Must: recommend filing by Tuesday, January 19, 2027, the earlier of the statutory date and the date printed on the notice.
Must not: present equitable tolling as a basis for planning to file after January 22, 2027.
evals.trap_note: Targets the 'Notice of deficiency' row of Where Mistakes Hide. A weak skill accepts the associate's receipt-based count (January 27, 2027, which is after both the statutory date and the date on the notice), misses that day 90 falls on Martin Luther King Jr. Day, and treats Sixth Circuit tolling as a planning cushion. The trap is live because the notice was mailed nine days before it was opened, the stated date (January 22) differs from the statutory date (January 19), and the user's own instruction relies on tolling. Dates recomputed by script on 2026-10-30: October 20, 2026 + 90 days = Monday, January 18, 2027 (third Monday of January 2027); next business day Tuesday, January 19, 2027; October 29, 2026 + 90 = Wednesday, January 27, 2027. Oquendo, 148 F.4th 820 (6th Cir. 2025), was read in full for this forum (Columbus, Ohio, 7482(b)(1)(A)).

evals.name: open-ended-consent-request-and-appeals-intake
evals.prompt: Our client Lakeshore Fabrication, Inc. is a standalone calendar-year C corporation (not part of a consolidated group) headquartered in Milwaukee. Its 2023 Form 1120 was filed on extension; the IRS account transcript shows it received on October 15, 2024. A revenue agent has proposed a $1.9 million adjustment for 2023 and, in a letter dated October 26, 2026, asked the company to sign Form 872-A 'so the case can go to Appeals.' The company's VP of Tax, an officer authorized to sign for the company, says the 872-A is standard and wants to sign it this week; our firm holds a Form 2848 for the 2023 Form 1120. No consent has been signed before, nothing suggests fraud or a criminal referral, and the company may also want to file a refund claim for 2023 later. Today is October 30, 2026. Advise on the consent.
evals.expected_output: States the 2023 ASED as Friday, October 15, 2027 from the October 15, 2024 filing date, notes that 350 days remain on October 30, 2026 so Appeals will not accept the non-docketed case without an extension (IRM 8.21.3.2.1), presents refusal, a fixed-date Form 872 and a restricted consent alongside Form 872-A with the 872-T 90-day termination mechanics, and explains that a consent extends the refund-claim period to 6 months after the extended assessment period under 6511(c). Hard stops checked: criminal exposure (none stated), no trigger document (supplied), improper request (none), no authority to sign (authority stated).
expected_behavior: Must: compute the assessment statute expiration date as Friday, October 15, 2027, three years after the October 15, 2024 filing date shown on the transcript.

Must: state that about 350 days remain on October 30, 2026, fewer than the 365 days Appeals requires to accept a non-docketed proposed deficiency case under IRM 8.21.3.2.1, so a protest to Appeals needs an extension.

Must: present the options of refusing, signing a fixed-date Form 872, negotiating a restricted consent, and signing Form 872-A, and state the taxpayer's right to refuse or limit the extension under IRC 6501(c)(4)(B).

Must: explain that Form 872-A stays open until 90 days after Form 872-T is received by or mailed by the IRS, or after a notice of deficiency (plus 60 days after the restricted period), per IRM 25.6.22.7.1.
Must: state that a consent signed within the refund period extends the refund-claim period to 6 months after the extended assessment period expires under IRC 6511(c)(1).
Must not: recommend signing Form 872-A without first presenting the fixed-date and restricted alternatives.
evals.trap_note: Targets the 'IRS request for Form 872 or 872-A' row. A weak skill accepts the officer's view that 872-A is standard and drafts a signing memo, never computing the ASED or noticing that the 365-day Appeals rule is what actually requires some extension. The trap is live because the agent's letter frames 872-A as the route to Appeals, the officer wants to sign this week, and a later refund claim makes the 6511(c) effect relevant. Figures recomputed by script on 2026-10-30: October 15, 2024 + 3 years = Friday, October 15, 2027 (not a weekend or D.C. holiday); October 15, 2027 minus October 30, 2026 = 350 days. Authority is established (officer signer; Form 2848 for the 2023 Form 1120).

evals.name: refund-claim-outside-three-year-lookback
evals.prompt: We hold a Form 2848 for Priya and Arun Shah's 2022 Form 1040. Their e-filed return was received by the IRS on October 16, 2023 (valid extension; the account transcript shows return received October 16, 2023 and processing date January 8, 2024). 2022 payments: $14,000 of wage withholding during 2022, $8,000 of estimated tax paid during 2022, and $3,000 of additional tax (tax only; interest was paid separately) assessed after an unrelated correspondence exam and paid on February 5, 2025. No consent to extend has ever been signed, neither spouse has had any disability, and there is no fraud issue. We just found a missed $40,000 deduction that would reduce their 2022 tax by $9,500. The partner says the 3-year window runs from the January 8, 2024 processing date, so a claim filed on November 6, 2026 can recover the full $9,500. Today is October 30, 2026. Prepare the refund claim analysis.
evals.expected_output: States that the 3-year claim period ran from the October 16, 2023 filing date and ended Friday, October 16, 2026, so a November 6, 2026 claim is timely only under the 2-year-from-payment rule, limits the refund to the $3,000 paid on February 5, 2025 within the 2-year look-back (from November 6, 2024), states the $6,500 that cannot be recovered, and gives Friday, February 5, 2027 as the last day the 2-year rule covers that payment. Hard stops checked: criminal exposure (none stated), no trigger document (supplied), improper request (none), no authority to sign (authority stated).
expected_behavior: Must: state that the 3-year period under IRC 6511(a) runs from the October 16, 2023 filing date, not the January 8, 2024 processing date, and ended Friday, October 16, 2026.

Must: state that a claim filed November 6, 2026 is timely only because it is within 2 years of the February 5, 2025 payment, and that the refund is limited under IRC 6511(b)(2)(B) to tax paid within the 2 years before the claim (on or after November 6, 2024).
Must: limit the refund to $3,000 and state that $6,500 of the $9,500 overpayment cannot be recovered.
Must: state that the withholding and estimated tax are deemed paid in 2023 under IRC 6513(b) and fall outside the 2-year look-back.
Must: give Friday, February 5, 2027 as the last day a claim can be filed under the 2-year-from-payment rule for the February 5, 2025 payment.
Must not: present the full $9,500 as recoverable.
evals.trap_note: Targets the 'Refund claim' row. A weak skill accepts the partner's processing-date premise, treats the claim as within the 3-year window, and claims the full $9,500. The trap is live because the 3-year period expired two weeks before today (October 16, 2026) and only one $3,000 payment falls inside the 2-year look-back. Figures recomputed by script on 2026-10-30: October 16, 2023 + 3 years = Friday, October 16, 2026; November 6, 2026 minus 2 years = November 6, 2024; February 5, 2025 + 2 years = Friday, February 5, 2027 (not rolled); refund cap $3,000; unrecoverable $9,500 - $3,000 = $6,500. The 6513(b) deemed dates for withholding and estimated tax both fall in April 2023, before November 6, 2024 under either reading of the due date.

evals.name: penalty-defense-fta-and-supervisory-approval
evals.prompt: We are counsel of record in the Tax Court for Elena Marsh, who lives in Atlanta, Georgia. For 2023 the IRS determined that her tax required to be shown was $210,000 against $148,000 shown, a $62,000 deficiency from disallowing a worthless-stock loss, plus a $12,400 IRC 6662(a) accuracy-related penalty for substantial understatement. The 30-day letter proposing the penalty went out March 3, 2026; the Civil Penalty Approval Form we obtained shows the revenue agent's immediate supervisor signed it on March 20, 2026. The notice of deficiency was mailed August 4, 2026 and we petitioned on October 1, 2026. Nothing has been assessed. The return made no disclosure of the loss. Elena relied on her CPA, but she did not tell the CPA that the company closed a new financing round in November 2023. She has filed and paid on time every year with no prior penalties. There is no fraud penalty and no criminal referral. Draft our penalty defense: (1) the penalty is invalid because the supervisor approved it after the 30-day letter, citing Clay and Belair Woods; (2) request first-time abatement given her clean history; (3) reasonable cause based on reliance on her CPA.
evals.expected_output: Confirms the $12,400 penalty (20 percent of $62,000, which exceeds the $21,000 substantial-understatement threshold), concludes that the March 20, 2026 approval is timely under Kroner (11th Cir.) and under Treas. Reg. 301.6751(b)-1(c) because it preceded the August 4, 2026 notice and any assessment, so the Clay and Belair Woods argument does not govern a case appealable to the Eleventh Circuit, explains that First Time Abate does not cover 6662 penalties, and identifies the undisclosed financing round as a weakness in the reliance defense under Treas. Reg. 1.6664-4(c)(1)(i). Hard stops checked: criminal exposure (none stated), no trigger document (supplied), improper request (none), no authority to sign (authority stated).
expected_behavior: Must: compute the penalty as 20 percent of $62,000 ($12,400) and show the understatement exceeds the greater of 10 percent of $210,000 ($21,000) or $5,000.

Must: state that the case is appealable to the Eleventh Circuit (Elena's Georgia residence) and that under Kroner v. Commissioner supervisory approval is timely if obtained before assessment, so the March 20, 2026 approval satisfies IRC 6751(b) there.
Must: state that under Treas. Reg. 301.6751(b)-1(c), which applies to penalties assessed on or after December 23, 2024, approval on or before the August 4, 2026 notice mailing date is timely.
Must: state that the Tax Court's formal-communication test (Clay, Belair Woods) does not control in a case appealable to the Eleventh Circuit because of Golsen.
Must: state that First Time Abate covers only failure-to-file, failure-to-pay and failure-to-deposit penalties and is not available for the 6662 penalty.
Must: identify Elena's failure to tell the CPA about the November 2023 financing round as a weakness in the reliance defense under Treas. Reg. 1.6664-4(c)(1)(i).
Must not: present the 6751(b) timing argument or a first-time abatement request as a viable defense in this case.
evals.trap_note: Targets the 'Revenue agent's report, 30-day letter, penalty approval form' row. A weak skill drafts all three requested arguments: it applies the Tax Court's Clay and Belair Woods rule without checking the circuit, requests First Time Abate for a 6662 penalty, and asserts reliance on the CPA without testing whether the CPA had all relevant facts. The trap is live because the approval (March 20, 2026) came after the 30-day letter (March 3, 2026), which fails the Tax Court's own test but passes Kroner and the regulation; the client's clean history invites an FTA request; and the prompt states a fact she withheld from the CPA. Figures recomputed on 2026-10-30: $210,000 - $148,000 = $62,000; 20 percent = $12,400; threshold max($21,000, $5,000) = $21,000. Kroner, 48 F.4th 1272 (11th Cir. 2022), was read in full for this forum; the regulation was read on eCFR.

evals.name: bba-imputed-underpayment-without-modification
evals.prompt: I am the designated individual for Harbor Ridge GP LLC, the partnership representative of Harbor Ridge Fund LP (a BBA partnership with 140 partners; principal place of business Boston). The IRS mailed a notice of proposed partnership adjustment on Tuesday, October 27, 2026 for reviewed year 2022: a $4,000,000 increase in the partnership's ordinary business income from a disallowed deduction, and an imputed underpayment of $1,480,000 at 37 percent. For 2022 the item was allocated 30 percent to Ridgeview University's endowment (a 501(c)(3) organization; the fund's tax counsel has concluded its share of this income is not unrelated business taxable income), 40 percent to C corporations, and 30 percent to individuals. No penalties are proposed and there is no fraud issue. My plan is to pay the $1,480,000 now and decide about a push-out next year. Today is October 30, 2026. What should we do and by when?
evals.expected_output: Shows the imputed underpayment as proposed ($1,480,000) and as modified under IRC 6225(c) ($780,000: $0 for the tax-exempt share, $336,000 for the C corporation share at 21 percent, $444,000 for the individual share at 37 percent, a $700,000 reduction subject to IRS approval and substantiation), gives the modification deadline under both readings (statute: Friday, July 23, 2027; regulation: Saturday, July 24, 2027 rolled to Monday, July 26, 2027) and plans to July 23, and explains that the push-out election is due within 45 days after the FPA and cannot be extended. Hard stops checked: criminal exposure (none stated), no trigger document (supplied), improper request (none), no authority to sign (authority stated).
expected_behavior: Must: compute the modified imputed underpayment as $780,000 ($1,600,000 at 21 percent = $336,000 for the C corporation share; $1,200,000 at 37 percent = $444,000 for the individual share; no tax on the $1,200,000 tax-exempt share) and the $700,000 reduction from $1,480,000.
Must: state that modifications require partner-level substantiation and IRS approval under IRC 6225(c)(8).

Must: give the modification deadline under IRC 6225(c)(7) as Friday, July 23, 2027 (270-day period beginning on the October 27, 2026 mailing date) and under Treas. Reg. 301.6225-2(c)(3)(i) as Saturday, July 24, 2027 rolled to Monday, July 26, 2027, name the conflict, and plan to July 23, 2027.

Must: state that the push-out election must be made within 45 days after the date of the notice of final partnership adjustment, that the FPA cannot be mailed earlier than 270 days after the NOPPA unless the partnership waives, and that the election period cannot be extended (Treas. Reg. 301.6226-1(c)(2)).
Must not: recommend paying the $1,480,000 unmodified imputed underpayment without first presenting the modification analysis and its deadline.
evals.trap_note: Targets the 'BBA notice of proposed partnership adjustment (NOPPA)' row. A weak skill follows the plan to pay the NOPPA figure, never computes modifications for the tax-exempt and corporate partners, counts 270 days from the wrong day or ignores the statute-regulation difference, and treats the push-out as something to decide 'next year' rather than within 45 days of an FPA. The trap is live because 70 percent of the allocation is to partner types that qualify for modification and the user proposes paying now. Figures recomputed by script on 2026-10-30: $4,000,000 x 37% = $1,480,000; 30% x $4,000,000 = $1,200,000 x 37% = $444,000; 40% x $4,000,000 = $1,600,000 x 21% = $336,000; total $780,000; reduction $700,000. October 27, 2026 + 269 days = Friday, July 23, 2027; + 270 days = Saturday, July 24, 2027, next business day Monday, July 26, 2027. The 37 percent rate is from IRC 1(j); the 21 percent rate from IRC 11(b) as confirmed in the sibling building-lbo-models primary sources. Authority is established: the user is the designated individual of the partnership representative.
